In phone surveys of Toronto and Vancouver residents (1984 to 1985; Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler, American Economic Review, 1986), a hardware store raising snow shovels from $15 to $20 the morning after a snowstorm was rated unfair by 82%. A grocer passing on a 30 cent a head wholesale rise for lettuce: 79% acceptable. A landlord raising rent at renewal to cover higher costs: 75% acceptable.

Pricing Clinic, Lesson 6: the note (example).
Starting next month, our rates are going up.

Anything you've already approved stays at the price we quoted.

Why the last line: repricing peanut butter already on the shelf when the wholesale price rose was rated unfair by 79%.
The catch: the study measured what people called fair, not what they bought. It can't promise you keep every customer.

youtube.title: How to Raise Prices With a Reason People Rated Acceptable (Plumbing, HVAC, Roofing)
youtube.description:
How to raise prices with a reason: a price increase note for plumbing, HVAC and roofing owners.
For home service and contractor business owners.
Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler, "Fairness as a Constraint on Profit Seeking: Entitlements in the Market," American Economic Review 76(4), September 1986. Telephone surveys of randomly selected residents of Toronto and Vancouver, May 1984 to July 1985:
A hardware store raises snow shovels from $15 to $20 the morning after a large snowstorm: 82% unfair (N = 107).
A grocer pays 30 cents a head more for lettuce and raises the price 30 cents: 79% acceptable (N = 101).
A landlord raises the rent at renewal to cover cost increases: 75% acceptable (N = 151).
A store raises the price on peanut butter already in stock the moment the wholesale price rises: 79% unfair (N = 147).
The study measured judgments of fairness, not purchases, so it can't promise you keep every customer.

Your price note (example):
1. Starting next month, our rates are going up.
2. Our labor and material costs went up this year.
3. Anything you've already approved stays at the price we quoted.

Send this to whoever sets your prices, before your next raise.
Next lesson: another Pricing Clinic fix for your prices.
